doc.title: Jim Cullum interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Time machine: King Oliver's band and the Snake Rag tribute
summary: Cullum recounts Eddie Condon hearing Oliver and Armstrong and a radio tribute switching from the old record to live playing.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: Okay here’s a little scenario. The time machine is a reality. Could you pick a couple of times that you’d like to go back to and be around when something happened in jazz history?

Well let me tell you. Everybody that plays this game, right, everybody that’s a jazz lover and a jazz fan, has these little — plays this little game in their head. And you go back and you think, and ‘cause Eddie Condon writes in this book and it says and so and he says so © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-

he meets Bix and Bix says he wants to go down to hear King Oliver. So they all go to hear King Oliver and they go down there and they stand there and Eddie Condon hadn’t been there himself. And he says and so one of the guys says the big guy, that’s Oliver, and that other guy’s just come from New Orleans, that’s the little guy, and his name is Armstrong and his name is Armstrong. That’s Armstrong. And so then they started to play and he said and these two cornets were playing like a couple of women talking over the back fence and they were, all the music was winding around each other, and it was pouring off, I mean he used this great rhetoric, it was pouring over like warm cream and flowing down through the holes and all this, I don’t know, you’d have to read Condon’s words. But so everybody that’s old would say all you hear is these old acoustic recordings of Oliver, of this thing. I would like to have gone and stood before the Oliver band, who George Wetting said would sometimes play one tune for half an hour and all the ensemble playing so they’d have to be real strong, and so I’d like to go and stand in front of this thing and hear what that really sounded like. So we did, on one of our shows, we’re doing a tribute to King Oliver so we had to get an extra cornet player, a real good guy from California, a tuba player, and the rhythm section to play kind of in this Oliver style a little bit, adjusted just slightly — it had a few peculiarities that were typical, and here we go. And so the Oliver band that the acoustic record is playing, the original record is playing, “Snake Rag.” “Snake Rag” has these little descending passages in it. And it’s an original piece by Joe Oliver. And the thing comes along [scats] and it has a run [scats] it goes along like this. Okay so we let the thing play about a minute and a half. And it finally comes to one of these passages and the thing goes live see? On the radio. And all of a sudden now you have modern electronics, here it is, and it sounds so great, ‘cause now it’s not muffled through the acoustic recording anymore. Here is the way it really sounded you know. So when you talk about going in the time machine, we’ve done it.
